samples.name: ordinary-php-handler.php
samples.identity: Minimal PHP POST command webshell with ordinary PHP handler configuration
trace: On every page request, file_put_contents overwrites adjacent .htaccess with a FilesMatch regex for .php and the PHP handler. Newlines are real newlines inside the PHP single-quoted string.

If POST job exists, its unfiltered value is argument zero of proc_open. A string command is shell-interpreted, allowing arbitrary commands as the PHP server account. There is no authentication, allowlist or escaping in this complete artifact.

Descriptor zero is a child-readable pipe; descriptor one is a child-writable pipe. stream_get_contents reads parent-side handles[1], echo returns stdout to the HTTP caller, and proc_close waits for the child. Stdin is not written or closed explicitly; commands waiting for stdin may block. Stderr is not captured.

Normal .php handler configuration is not extension masquerading or evidence of persistence. No decoding, obfuscation, credential theft, reverse connection, privilege escalation or payload download exists.
samples.coverage_gap: One hostile request-command-output interface is supported. Three suspicious findings describe the same boundary crossing; a second distinct hostile behavior would be invented or duplicated, so none was added.

samples.name: filesmatch-console.php
samples.identity: PHP POST command webshell with Apache data-file execution mapping
trace: Same complete command and stdout path as ordinary-php-handler.php, with one content change: the FilesMatch suffix is .dat.

The unconditional adjacent .htaccess write maps data-named .dat files to PHP execution with a compatible Apache PHP handler and allowed overrides. This extends the command backdoor with data-file execution configuration.
No .dat payload is written or restored by this file. Existing rules correctly describe co-occurrence with a command webshell, not a demonstrated restored file or persistent activation.
samples.coverage: Three retained hostile findings describe the request command/output channel and the associated data-file handler configuration; no distinct behavior was manufactured.

samples.name: report-upload.ps1
samples.identity: Archibus DWR authentication-bypass and JSPX upload exploit client
trace: Accepts operator BaseUrl; constructs a literal single-quoted here-string with three serialized RPC calls and POSTs it to BaseUrl.TrimEnd slash plus /custom/dwr/call/plaincall/Multiple.3.dwr as text/plain.

Call zero is SecurityService.getProjects. Call one is SecurityService.isPasswordUppercase for fixture-project. Call two is workflow.runWorkflowRule selecting AbCommonResources-writeHTMLtoFile. Calls are ordered in a single DWR batch.

The html field references c2-e1, which contains well-formed JSPX with a Date constructor expression; fileExtension references c2-e2, exactly string:jspx. A normal report does not need executable JSPX or an inherited pre-auth privileged context.

Rapid7 original research explains the vulnerable password-check method setting a core user session in thread-local ContextStore, reused by the next workflow call; writeHTMLtoFile writes supplied content with the supplied suffix. This is independently consistent with the source, not a conviction based on an advisory mentioning the hash.

The JSPX only renders a date. No shell, credential read, persistence, returned filename parsing or follow-up fetch occurs. The script submits an exploit-stage file-write request and does not itself activate the JSPX.

Hard-coded fixture project and session ID may prevent success; getProjects output is not captured or substituted. A valid BaseUrl, vulnerable endpoint, project/session data and suitable server configuration remain prerequisites. Static evidence establishes the attempted exploit without proving success.
The XML namespace HTTP URL is a schema identifier, not a contacted C2 endpoint. page=%2F is protocol serialization, not evasion. No hidden or additional encoded payload appears in facts.
